Turkey and Qatar have signed a mutual defence agreement in Istanbul on Friday, in what is the latest military pact between Ankara and other Muslim states.
The defence agreement was one of five agreed between Turkey and Qatar, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan hosted the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
A statement by the Turkish president's office said that Friday's mutual defence agreement with Qatar "would add another dimension to our brotherhood".
Erdogan said Turkey and Qatar’s cooperation in the defence industry would continue to grow, according to the statement.
Turkey and Qatar have had several defence agrements since 2017, including the hosting of Turkish troops in Doha, but the new deal obliged both countries to come to the other's defence.
In August this year, Turkey signed a defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, known as the Mecca Agreement.
Last week, the Turkish parliament passed a law approving the Mecca defence pact early on Friday, completing a crucial stage in the legal process.
The move will allow the deployment of Turkish troops to Saudi Arabia, which is currently at war with Yemen's Houthis.
In October, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said that any deployment to Saudi Arabia would be defensive in nature and that Turkish forces would not operate in Yemen.

The large studios of Abdul Rahman Katanani and Ayman Baalbaki are filled with canvases and installations about memory and destruction, drawn from the Israeli wars that shaped both artists’ youth.
These magical spaces, one in an anonymous building in busy central Beirut, and the other far from the city in a village high in the hills, speak for Lebanon and Palestine.
They also define the two artists and their families.
Katanani’s materials are barbed wire, corrugated metal sheets, olive branches, petroleum barrels and discarded clothes from his birthplace, the Sabra and Shatila refugee camp.
“I’ve always wanted to use the materials of the camp. These materials are our shadows. No... they’re us,” he told Middle East Eye.
The harsh materials yield startling lyrical shapes, such as a nine-metre wave in barbed wire, a child playing, a lotus flower and a bright early collage of clothes, including the unexpectedly intimate detail of underwear.
Once, he built a replica of the Palestinian camp of his childhood, shown inside an art gallery.
Ayman Baalbaki in his studio (Victoria Brittain/MEE)

The United Arab Emirates remains the key trading hub for smuggled gold and conflict gold, a new report from Switzerland’s Swissaid foundation has found.
Despite the introduction in 2023 of legislation intended to curb illegal flows, the UAE, which is now the world’s second largest gold trading hub after Switzerland, imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024.
Illicit gold refers to that which was either smuggled to the UAE - most often to the gold markets of Dubai, the second largest Emirate - without being able to be traced, or that comes from countries at war, including Yemen, Sudan and Russia.
The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa, according to Swissaid. It also continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions.
“The findings of this study are deeply concerning. They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold,” said Marc Ummel, head of Swissaid’s commodities unit and co-author of the study.
In 2024, the UAE imported at least 174.5 tonnes of gold from Russia (directly and indirectly via Armenia), Yemen and Sudan (directly and indirectly), Swissaid found. The entire volume from these three countries can, the organisation said, “be considered as conflict gold”.
Gold and war
The UAE has been directly involved in both the wars in Yemen and Sudan, where it is the patron of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group widely determined to have committed genocide in different parts of Darfur.

A senior Chabad rabbi has been criticised by his own movement after he said it was permissible to kill Jewish Israeli politicians who worked with Arabs.
Gedalia Axelrod, a senior cleric in the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, issued a halakhic ruling earlier this week in which he said that Jewish politicians who form a government backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel were "din rodef", which roughly translates as "law of the pursuer".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary.
The doctrine was previously invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".
Collaboration could either take the form of inviting Arab parties to join a governing coalition, or even relying on their support from outside it.
Swift condemnation
Axelrod's comments were swiftly condemned by the leadership of his religious movement, with Chabad spokesperson Rabbi Shimi Segal clarifying that his statements did not represent the official Chabad position.
“Chabad’s official halachic positions are determined exclusively by the Chabad Rabbinical Court, in accordance with the Rebbe’s instructions,” he said.

Israel is extending its $3,500 voluntary departure grant to nationals of every African country in a bid to reverse a decline in the number of migrants leaving with state assistance, according to Haaretz.
Until now the payment had been limited mainly to people from a handful of states.
The change took effect on Monday and will remain in place until the end of the year, Israel's Population and Immigration Authority said. Applications must be submitted by 31 December.
It covers African nationals who have stayed in Israel for more than two years without a valid visa, and those holding temporary residency permits.
For the first time, it also includes people who entered Israel legally but overstayed their visas.
The authority expects several thousand more people to be eligible, including citizens of Nigeria, South Africa and Togo.
Before the change, the grant was mostly open to people who crossed into Israel outside official border points. That group includes nationals of Eritrea, Sudan, Ethiopia, Ivory Coast and Guinea, along with citizens of countries that have no diplomatic relations with Israel.
The authority’s figures show that 3,511 African nationals left with help from its Voluntary Departure Unit in 2024. That fell to 2,815 in 2025, a drop of about 20 percent.

It was half past five in the afternoon when Bahij Abdallah saw a white object pass overhead.
He was outside a pumping station in Ebel el-Saqi, in the hills above Marjayoun, checking on an open water reservoir. He had sat down on a stone step with his phone in his hand, while three colleagues remained inside.
At first, he thought the white thing was a drone.
“Suddenly, it stopped in the air for a second, turned, and fell on the station,” Abdallah told Middle East Eye. “Then the smoke and the fire started.”
The phone flew out of his hand. He felt a wall of air, and then metal pushing into his body. He looked down and saw blood dripping from his face. His shoulder was burning. When he stood up, he saw that his shoe had been cut open.
Abdallah, an electrical maintenance employee with the South Lebanon Water Establishment (SLWE), the state utility that supplies drinking water to two governorates, had been doing what he does most days: running the station and monitoring it.

In the filing, seen by AFP, the rights group says that marketing Israeli settlements in the occupied territories contributes to the forced displacement of the Palestinian people through population transfer - a practice prohibited by international law and classified as a war crime under the French penal code.
In particular, the activists highlighted that BH Nadlan, a company that markets settlements in both East Jerusalem and the West Bank on its website, will be present at the fair.
They also pointed to the fair's official guide's offer of a "significant" financial "bonus" for newcomers settling in "Judea and Samaria", the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.

Six political parties in the Dutch city of Tilburg have condemned a local arms company’s deal with Israeli gunmaker Israel Weapon Industries (IWI).
The parties have asked the municipal authorities whether they can prevent weapons produced under the agreement from reaching Israel’s military and whether they can block local production.
Tilburg-based AIA bought designs and technical know-how from IWI and plans to make rifles and light machine guns at an industrial park in the city.
The agreement covers the Arad 5 infantry rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun. Production will initially take place in Tilburg before moving to a larger site in Overijssel, according to Dutch broadcaster Omroep Brabant.
AIA says that it intends to supply European countries and other Nato partners. It remains unclear whether the company could also sell the weapons to Israel.
D66, PRO, Denk, the Party for the Animals, the Socialist Party and VoorTilburg013 submitted questions to the municipal administration.
In a statement, D66 councillor Sofia Schampers said: “We refuse to stand tacitly by while Tilburg potentially contributes to the genocide of the Palestinian people.”

Saar made the comments following a meeting with a visting delegation from the British Conservative Party on Wednesday evening in Jerusalem.

'We lost patients I had been caring for': Nasser nurse speaks of 'terrifying' attack
A nurse who was working a night shift at Nasser Hospital's surgical department when it was targeted by an Israeli air strike has said that a number of patients they were caring for were killed in the attack.
In testimony shared by the NGO Medical Aid for Palestine (MAP), Mohammed Salman described the attack on the hospital, which is the largest in southern Gaza, as "terrifying".
"I saw patients trapped under the rubble and colleagues injured. We lost some of the patients I had been caring for, including at least two," he said.
"Our greatest fear was for the patients. We immediately started trying to evacuate them and get them to safety, working alongside Civil Defence teams and moving those we could rescue to another department."
Salman said a colleague, surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaeria, was killed as he was checking on a patient.
"A few minutes later, everything changed, and we lost him. It is incredibly painful to lose a colleague who was simply doing his job and dedicating himself to caring for patients," he said.
In a statement, the Palestinian Ministry of Health reported that two missiles struck the upper floors of the hospital's Yassin building, which houses the surgical department, at around 00:39 local time, killing six – including surgeons, patients and a child. It added that one of the missiles failed to detonate and remains inside the building, posing an additional threat to patients and medical staff still there.
Nasser Hospital is one of the few still able to provide care. According to the UN's OCHA, just 20 of the Strip's 37 hospitals remain partially functional and none are fully functional.

Republicans in the US House of Representatives blocked an attempt to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on Tuesday, sparking a flurry of criticism online, as 11 Democrats failed to attend the vote.
The chamber voted 211 to 204 to refer the charges to the House Judiciary Committee, where they could remain indefinitely for the duration of this Congress’s term, essentially killing the resolution for now.
The articles were spearheaded by Republican Thomas Massie and backed heavily by Democrats, accusing Hegseth of carrying out unlawful orders and waging unconstitutional wars in Iran and Venezuela.
Notably, there were 18 representatives missing during the votes - seven Republicans and 11 Democrats. The Democrats missing included California's Nancy Pelosi; Michigan’s Haley Stevens; New York’s Laura Gillen; California’s Lou Correa; New Mexico’s Melanie Stansbury; and several others.

El-Quseir is pitch black at night. The only light inside this decaying labyrinth of a port comes when a battered Bajaj motorcycle purrs down the odd alley, casting a headlight on one of the town’s many stray dogs, or a passerby flashes a phone, lighting up a decaying wooden balcony.
The old mayor’s house is easy to find in the darkness. It emits a warm, golden light. When I arrive, a crowd is already gathered on the colonnaded veranda; some men in djellabas, others in the uniform skinny jeans of the Middle East.
I spot the odd Cairo hipster among them. The women attendees are especially radiant in make-up. Why shouldn’t they be.
Tonight is a Hazz night, the name, which in Arabic means luck, given to soirees down Egypt’s Red Sea coast, where the simsimiyya , a triangular lyre, is played to ballads about old ports, friendships and legendary seafarers.
The simsimiyya looms large over El-Quseir.
“The men here would be at sea for four months at a time. They would save a spot on their dhow just for a simsimiyya player to entertain them,” Aly El-Sayed, the founder of Bahar, a community organisation working to preserve the city's heritage and marine ecosystem, told me.
Aly is the host of tonight’s gathering. The old mayor’s house, a butter-yellow bungalow built in 1888, has been repurposed as Bahar’s home.
“We tried not to change much. We were even careful not to paint too much,” El-Sayed said.
'They sang all the time'
I knew that music was central to life aboard dhows, traditional wooden sailing boats, that plied goods, including slaves, between East Africa and Arabia up until the mid-20th century.

“The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us. This is the path to mutually assured destruction,” UN secretary general Antonio Guterres told world leaders at the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey on Wednesday.
The UN chief siad that the slow international response to the climate crisis had put the world on this path and that rapid action was needed to avert it.
His comments set the tone for two days of rapid-fire speeches by world leaders at the UN conference on Turkey's Mediterranean coast, Reuters reported.
Guterres pointed to rising carbon emissions, global temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters in his speech.
“But science is not telling us to surrender. It is telling us to fight harder,” he said. “Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs.”
Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are seeking agreement on a plan to increase the share of electricity in global energy use and revive stalled efforts to move away from fossil fuels.
The summit opened on Monday and has, relative to its importance, received little attention against a backdrop of numerous wars, rampant inflation and other crises.

after.summary:
UKMTO reports tanker incident in Hormuz Strait
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said it received the report of an incident involving a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz.
It added that the status of the crew, the extent of any damage and the environmental impact were not yet known.
